planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana trillium is a Mississippi Delta and Gulf Coastal Plain sessile species that thrives in the same rich, seasonally flooded hardwood terraces as spring ephemerals like trout lily and bloodroot.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana trillium is a Mississippi Delta and Gulf Coastal Plain sessile species that thrives in the same rich, seasonally flooded hardwood terraces as spring ephemerals like trout lily and bloodroot. Closely related to the more widespread Trillium cuneatum, it produces broad silver-mottled leaves in a whorl of three beneath a stalkless, upright flower whose narrow maroon-to-bronze petals appear in late winter to early spring, well before the deciduous canopy leafs out. It is one of the few trilliums reliably suited to warm, humid Gulf South gardens rather than cooler Appalachian conditions, making it a good match for shaded beds under live oak or hackberry from Louisiana into coastal Texas and Mississippi. Top-dress with leaf mold each fall and avoid summer irrigation once the foliage yellows and goes dormant, since the dormant rhizome prefers to dry out somewhat during the hot months.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, rich, well-drained alluvial soil in partial to full shade; this Louisiana endemic grows naturally on the low hardwood ridges and terraces bordering the Atchafalaya Basin and appreciates the same seasonally damp, leaf-litter-covered ground.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, rich, well-drained alluvial soil in partial to full shade; this Louisiana endemic grows naturally on the low hardwood ridges and terraces bordering the Atchafalaya Basin and appreciates the same seasonally damp, leaf-litter-covered ground. Its broad, heavily silver-mottled leaves and sessile maroon-to-yellow-green flowers closely resemble those of Trillium cuneatum, but the common name refers to the faint carrion scent the flowers give off to draw in the small flies and beetles that pollinate them. Extremely restricted in the wild to a handful of south Louisiana parishes, it is best sourced only from nurseries growing seed-propagated stock, and makes a conversation-starting addition to a shaded native bed already hosting spider lilies or Louisiana iris. Once established the clump slowly bulks up by offsets and needs little more than an annual leaf-mold top-dressing and protection from summer waterlogging.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, acidic to circumneutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; slender trillium is native to the pine-hardwood bottomlands of eastern Texas and western Louisiana and prefers the same dappled light and steady leaf-litter moisture.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, acidic to circumneutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; slender trillium is native to the pine-hardwood bottomlands of eastern Texas and western Louisiana and prefers the same dappled light and steady leaf-litter moisture. It is one of the narrower-petaled members of the mottled-leaf trillium group, with long, slim maroon to greenish-bronze petals held erect above three broadly mottled leaves, flowering in late winter into early spring. Its more delicate, upright habit compared to the stockier Trillium cuneatum suits a shaded woodland border where it can be viewed up close, and it pairs well with other Piney Woods natives like woodland phlox and Louisiana iris. Leave the clump undisturbed once planted, since trillium rhizomes resent being moved and take several seasons to recover their full flowering vigor after transplant.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Texas trillium is native to damp baygalls and seepage-slope pine-hardwood forest of the western Gulf Coastal Plain and needs steadier moisture than most upland trilliums.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Texas trillium is native to damp baygalls and seepage-slope pine-hardwood forest of the western Gulf Coastal Plain and needs steadier moisture than most upland trilliums. Unlike its mottled-leaved cousins, it carries plain green leaves and a pedicellate, nodding-to-erect white flower that ages to pink, blooming in early spring in the wet, acidic soils of southeast Texas and adjacent Louisiana. Rare and highly localized in the wild, it is best grown from nursery-propagated stock in a shaded bog garden or the damp margin of a rain garden alongside pitcher plants, sundews, or Virginia sweetspire. Keep the soil reliably moist through the growing season and mulch with pine straw to hold moisture and mimic its native acidic litter layer.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, limestone-derived soil in partial to full shade; green trillium is endemic to the Edwards Plateau of central Texas, where it grows in the leaf litter of oak-juniper canyons over limestone bedrock.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, limestone-derived soil in partial to full shade; green trillium is endemic to the Edwards Plateau of central Texas, where it grows in the leaf litter of oak-juniper canyons over limestone bedrock. Its sessile flowers open a striking yellow-green and hold three broadly mottled leaves close to the ground, blooming from late winter into early spring before the surrounding oak canopy fills in. As a limestone-country endemic it is fussier about drainage and pH than Gulf Coast trilliums, so a raised bed amended with crushed limestone or decomposed granite alongside the humus works better than a heavy, poorly drained clay border. Water well through fall and spring, then let the ground dry out somewhat as the plant goes summer-dormant, matching the Hill Country's naturally dry summers.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; lanceleaf trillium is native to calcareous bluffs and ravines of the Deep South, from Georgia and Alabama into the Florida panhandle, and does best tucked among rocks or roots that keep its roots cool.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; lanceleaf trillium is native to calcareous bluffs and ravines of the Deep South, from Georgia and Alabama into the Florida panhandle, and does best tucked among rocks or roots that keep its roots cool. It is easy to tell apart from other sessile trilliums by its narrow, lance-shaped leaves, which are only lightly mottled compared to the broad, heavily marbled foliage of Trillium cuneatum, above a small sessile maroon-to-bronze flower in early spring. Its compact, low-growing habit and tolerance of thin, rocky, well-drained soil make it a good fit for a shaded rock garden or a bluff-style planting along a slope, rather than the deep, rich woodland loam most trilliums prefer. Give it excellent drainage year-round and resist the urge to water it through summer dormancy, since standing moisture on the bluff-adapted rhizome is a common cause of rot.
